messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Housekeeper
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 61

**Patient Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 32-year-old married South Asian man who presents for an initial consultation at the urging of his wife. He speaks quietly, often pausing to look at the floor, his hands resting motionless on his knees. He works as a housekeeper for a large hotel chain, a job he held for three years before the event.

The trauma occurred eight months ago. Mr. A. was walking home from the evening bus stop, a ten-minute route he had taken hundreds of times. It was just past 11 p.m., and the street was unusually empty. Two men approached him from behind. One pressed a hard object into his lower back. They demanded his wallet and phone. Mr. A. remembers the cold, precise pressure of the object, the smell of cigarette smoke and sweat on the man’s jacket. He handed over everything. They shoved him to the ground, and one of them kicked his ribs before they ran off. He lay on the pavement for what felt like a long time, unable to move, his breath coming in short, sharp gasps. He remembers the wetness of the asphalt against his cheek.

In the weeks that followed, Mr. A. tried to return to his normal routine. He did not report the incident to the police. He told himself it was over, that he was lucky to be unharmed. But he could not stop the replaying. The scene arrives without warning: the pressure in his back, the smell of smoke, the cold asphalt. It happens most often when he is alone, or in the quiet moments before sleep. He describes it as a “video that plays in my head,” one he cannot turn off. He feels the same terror, the same paralysis.

His work has become a minefield. The hotel’s hallways are long, carpeted, and often empty, especially on the early morning shift. He now walks with his back to the wall, his head turning constantly. He avoids the service elevator after a guest accidentally bumped into him from behind; he dropped his cart of linens and stood frozen for several minutes. His supervisor has noticed his slowness, his jumpiness. Mr. A. has started taking longer routes through the building, routes that allow him to see around corners. He is exhausted.

At home, the changes are stark. He and his wife used to cook together most evenings. Now, he cannot bear to stand with his back to the kitchen door. He sits facing the entrance of every room, and he startles violently if she enters a room without announcing herself. He has not slept through the night in five months. He wakes drenched in sweat, heart pounding, convinced he hears footsteps in the hallway. He has begun checking the locks on the apartment door three or four times before they go to bed. His wife, initially patient, has grown frustrated. She tells him he is “not the same person.” He agrees. He feels hollowed out, irritable, and disconnected from her. He has stopped calling his family in India; the thought of explaining his state feels impossible.

Mr. A. no longer takes the bus. He walks a longer, more circuitous route to work, one that avoids the street where the mugging occurred. He cannot go near that block. He feels a wave of nausea and a tightness in his chest if his bus route is diverted near the area. He has withdrawn from the small social circle he had at the hotel. He tells himself it is safer to be alone, that he cannot trust the quiet, that the world is simply not safe anymore. He spends his days off sitting in the living room, watching the door, waiting for nothing.
